Infused Righteousness
in-fuzd´ rīt´yus-nes
n. phrase (Rome's interior gift of justice, treated as the formal cause of justification; not the imputed righteousness of Christ)
Latin infundere, to pour in. Infused righteousness is justice poured into the soul as a habit. The Reformation's counter-word is imputed: counted, not poured, as the ground of the verdict.

Biblical Definition

Infused righteousness is the Roman account of how a man is made just: grace is poured into him, a habit of justice is created, and on that interior gift — with his cooperation — he is counted righteous. The Authorized Version locates the verdict elsewhere. “But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5). The man in view is ungodly when he is justified. A habit of justice cannot be the formal cause of that sentence. “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). Paul will not even let a Christian's own Spirit-wrought deeds into the ground: “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). He will be found “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ” (Php 3:9). And David describes “the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works” (Rom 4:6). Infusion as sanctification is not in dispute. Infusion as the thing that justifies is another gospel.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines infuse as to pour in, as a liquid, and to instill, as principles or qualities. Infused righteousness takes that pouring as the ground of God's verdict. The Scriptures use counting, not pouring, for that verdict.

expand to see more

INFU'SE, v.t. [L. infusus, infundo, to pour in; in and fundo, to pour.]

1. To pour in, as a liquid.

2. To instill, as principles or qualities.

4. To introduce; as, to infuse Gallicisms into a composition.

The theological phrase infused righteousness is not Webster's headword. It names Rome's poured interior justice as the formal cause of justification.

Key Scripture

Rom 4:5 — "But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness."

Rom 3:28 — "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law."

Gal 2:16 — "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified."

Php 3:9 — "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:"

Rom 4:6 — "Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,"

Modern Corruption

If the verdict waits on a poured quality, the ungodly cannot be justified, and Romans 4:5 has to be rewritten as a man already being made godly.

expand to see more

Trent made infused righteousness the formal cause of justification. The man is not counted just by Christ's righteousness extra nos. He is made just by a grace in him, and he must cooperate. Romans 4:5 will not survive that. God justifieth the ungodly. Faith is counted for righteousness to the man who worketh not. If a habit of justice were the cause, the man would not be ungodly at the moment of the verdict, and Paul would have said so.

Protestant slides toward the same place by making justification a process of becoming. Galatians 2:16 was written to people who already believed, to stop them adding the law back into the ground. Infused righteousness as sanctification is what the Spirit actually does. The corruption is using that real work as the title to the court. Philippians 3:9 keeps two righteousnesses distinct: mine own, of the law; and God's, through the faith of Christ. Mixing them is how you lose both the verdict and the holiness.

The pastoral fruit of the Roman construction is never-finished assurance. If the habit can be lost, the verdict can be lost. Romans 4:6's blessedness is without works. That is not a permission to be lawless. It is the only ground on which a man can then obey without using his obedience as currency.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin iustitia infusa; Greek logizomai (G3049), to count; dikaioō (G1344), to justify; asebēs (G765), ungodly.

expand to see more

Greek logizomai (G3049) — counted, imputed; Romans 4:5, 4:6 — the verb infusion cannot replace.

Greek asebē (G765) — the ungodly; Romans 4:5, the one God justifies.

Latin iustitia infusa — infused justice; Trent's formal cause, against the Protestant iustitia imputata.

Usage

"“Him that justifieth the ungodly” — not the man already made just inside."

"“Justified by faith without the deeds of the law” — including Spirit-assisted deeds as ground."

"“Imputeth righteousness without works” — counted, not poured, as the verdict."
